steps: Uncrate
Carefully remove the wood top and supports, then the plastic cover. Remove all screws holding the legs or pedestal to the pallet.
Floor protection & placement

On a combustible floor, lay UL 1618 Type 1 non-combustible ember protection (USA: 16" to the front of the firebox, 8" from the sides of the loading door opening; Canada: 18" / 8"). Position stove and protector, with the combustion-air hole if needed, to the label clearances.

On a combustible floor, use UL 1618 Type 1 ember protection of non-combustible material, the equivalent of 20 Gauge steel or tile.

USA16" (406 mm) to the front of the firebox · 8" (203 mm) from the sides of the fuel loading door opening
Canada18" (457 mm) from the loading door on the firing side · 8" (203 mm) from the sides

Position the stove and floor protection (with the hole for combustion air if required) to the clearances on the label and in Figure 7.

Securing brackets come bagged with the unit: slide them through the slots in the rear legs and lag them to the floor or hearth pad. Needed for mobile homes; recommended with outside air to stop the stove moving and the air intake separating.
Chimney through ceiling & roof

Follow the chimney maker's instructions: plumb-bob the hole, check joists and rafters, cut and frame, then fit the support, flashing and radiation shield with no chimney joints between ceiling and roof. Add the storm collar, sections to a safe height and the rain cap; check for leaks.

Follow the chimney manufacturer's instructions; the manual gives general steps only.

  1. Mark the ceiling and roof hole with a string and plumb-bob; check it clears floor joists, ceiling joists and rafters.
  2. Cut the hole, frame the sides and install the roof or ceiling support.
  3. Install the roof flashing; secure and seal it.
  4. Assemble the chimney sections resting on the support and through the roof; install the radiation shield. Avoid chimney joints between ceiling and roof.
  5. Install the storm collar and sections to a safe height, attach the rain cap and check the system for leaks.

Offsets: screw every connector, offset elbow and chimney joint with at least three sheet metal screws and support it with the chimney maker's listed offset support (Figure 6, p. 15).
Chimney connector

Listed double-wall connector to its maker's instructions, or 6"(150mm) minimum 24 gauge black pipe, clean, new, short and straight: crimped end down inside the stove collar, three screws at the collar and each joint. It must not pass through an attic, roof space, closet, floor or ceiling.
Masonry chimney option

Code-approved chimney with a listed flue liner, in good condition; flue or liner the same size as the stove outlet (a full stainless steel liner may help draft). Flue exit 3 feet above the roof and two feet above the highest projection within 10 feet; minimum system height 12 feet from the top of the appliance.
Combustible-wall pass-through

Maintain the vapor barrier. Use an NFPA 211 pass-through: System A (12 in. brick), B (listed insulated chimney length, 9 in. air space), C (ventilated thimble, 6 in. glass fiber insulation) or D (insulated chimney section, 2 in. air space).

Per NFPA 211-2013. The vapor barrier must be maintained wherever the chimney or other components penetrate to the exterior.

System A · 12 in.Min. 3.5 in. brick masonry wall, 12 in. of brick from clay liner to combustibles; fireclay liner min. 5/8 in. wall
System B · 9 in.Solid-insulated listed chimney length, same ID as the connector, 1 in. or more insulation, 9 in. air space to combustibles
System C · 6 in.Min. 24 gauge connector and ventilated thimble (two 1 in. air channels), 6 in. glass fiber insulation to combustibles
System D · 2 in.Solid-insulated listed chimney section 2 in. larger ID than the connector, min. 12 in. long, connector spaced 1 in., 2 in. air space

Supports fastened on all sides; fasteners must not penetrate the chimney liner.

Note: the manual allows passage through a combustible wall if the installation conforms to CAN/CSA-B365 or NFPA 211 on p. 14 (systems A–D on pp. 17–18), and the rating label says do not pass a chimney connector through a combustible wall or ceiling on p. 26.
Mobile home

Listed double-wall connector, 6"(150mm) listed connector and chimney, outside combustion air, and a chimney at least 12' (3.66 m) above the unit or per the chimney maker's roof clearances, whichever is greater. Keep the floor, wall and roof structure intact; lag the stove down with two 1/4" x 1" or longer lag screws.

Listed double-wall connector; connector and chimney 6"(150mm), listed to UL-103 HT (USA) or ULC S-641 / ULC-S-629 (Canada). Outside combustion air supply must be used.

  • Chimney: at least 12' (3.66 m) from the top of the unit, or the chimney maker's roof clearances if greater.
  • Attach the stove to the floor with two 1/4" x 1" or longer lag screws. Leg model: anchor tabs in the slots on the bottom of the two rear legs (Figure 5).
  • With the optional blower kit, the unit must be grounded to the mobile home.
  • Rating label: horizontal connector not permitted in mobile homes.
  • Clearances: double-wall close-clearance values on the rating label (p. 26); Figure 8 shows them as a drawing.
Combustion air

Outside air through the floor or the nearest exterior wall with the OAIR.1B adapter, 4"(100mm) metal venting, an approved inlet vent cap and 20GA minimum rodent screen; or room air by removing the knockout/cover plate. Secure the stove when using outside air.
Optional blower

Remove the two screws and cover plate from the rear shield, set the blower in with its outlet pointing up and fasten with the kit screws. 115V, 60Hz, 0.5 amps; route the three-prong cord away from the heater.
Firebrick & first-fire check
With the stove in its final position, fit the 20 firebricks: 4 under the rear brick rail, the floor bricks lengthwise (Figure 14), then 4 per side under the brick retainer.

The package contains 20 full-size firebricks (set 80000620, 9" x 4 1/2" x 1 1/4"). Install with the stove in its final position.

  1. Slide the first brick up under the rear brick rail to the far left or far right; add 3 more to complete the rear.
  2. Lay the floor bricks as shown in Figure 14.
  3. Each side: place the first side-wall brick under the brick retainer, on top of the floor bricks, and slide it back against the rear bricks; then 3 more along that wall.
Before the first fire, remove the retaining clip on the front of the baffle (p. 9). Do not operate with the baffle board insulation or tubes removed (p. 21).

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Before your very first fire, remove the retaining clip on the front of the baffle.

  1. Move the air control lever all the way to the left. That's the maximum firing rate. Open the door.
  2. Put crumpled newspaper in the centre of the firebox. Crisscross several pieces of dry kindling on top, then add a few small pieces of dry wood.
  3. Light the paper. Leave the door open about 1/2" to 1" until the kindling is fully in flames. Don't leave the stove unattended.
  4. Once the kindling is fully engulfed, add a few small logs and close the door.
  5. Start normal burning once you have a good bed of coals and the wood has charred.

Burn right on the firebricks. Don't raise the fire on a grate or andirons, and replace any broken or missing bricks.

Fire starters made from paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine for lighting.
Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or "freshen up" a fire. Keep them well away from the stove.

air.title: Burning, reloading and overnight burns
air.html:
The air control lever sets how hard the fire burns. All the way to the left is the maximum firing rate.

Everyday burning

  • Set the lever where you want it. Every home's heating needs differ, so find your setting by trial and error and note it for next time.
  • If smoke pours down across the glass (a "waterfall"), you turned the air down too soon or too low.

Reloading

  1. Move the air control to high and give the fire time to brighten.
  2. Open the door slowly. This stops smoke from puffing back into the room.
  3. Load dry wood of mixed shapes and sizes, placed so air can flow between the logs. Don't stack it so high that opening the door would be a hazard.

Overnight burns

Unsplit logs work best. Char the wood completely on the maximum setting before you turn the air down.

To restart, open the door and rake the hot embers to the front. Add a couple of dry, split logs, close the door and set the air to high. Once the wood has charred, reset the air.

Don't over-fire. Use the full-left setting only to start a fire or preheat a fresh load.
With the optional blower: except on its High setting, wait 30 minutes before turning it on.

wood.title: Choosing your wood
wood.html:
Burn only natural, seasoned cordwood. Air-dried hardwoods give higher efficiency and lower emissions than softwoods or green wood.

  • Season wood for six months or more. Store it under cover, away from open flame or heat.
  • Wet wood smoulders, makes lots of smoke and creosote, gives little heat and tends to go out.
  • 18" is the ideal log length; the loading instructions say to use wood up to 18" long. The manual's maximum wood length is 20 inches.
Maker's website: Log Size (max.) 18 in. That's the manual's ideal length; the manual's maximum is 20 inches.

Test a piece

Put a large piece on a good bed of coals. Dry wood burns on more than one side within one minute. Damp wood turns black and lights within three minutes. If it sizzles, hisses and blackens without lighting in five minutes, it's soaked. Don't burn it.

Never burn

Wet or green wood, unseasoned wood, treated or salt-water wood, coal or charcoal, garbage, lawn clippings or yard waste, railroad ties, manure or animal remains, cardboard or other paper products, plywood, particleboard, anything with plastic, rubber (including tires) or asbestos, waste petroleum products, paints, paint thinners, solvents, asphalt products, or construction or demolition debris. Burning these can release toxic fumes, or make the stove ineffective and cause smoke. Salt-water wood and garbage contain chlorides that destroy metal and void the warranty. Charcoal can give off large amounts of carbon monoxide, an odorless gas that can kill. Never barbecue in the stove.

Note: The do-not-burn list (p. 8) names wet or green wood and unseasoned wood, and the chimney-fire advice (p. 7) says not to burn wet wood. The safety section (p. 4) says that if you feel it is necessary to burn wet or unseasoned wood, do so only with the air inlet set open enough to keep a good, strong fire and fairly high chimney temperatures, and not to try to burn overnight with green or wet wood.

firstfire.title: Your first few fires
firstfire.html:
The paint on your stove bakes on during the first 2-3 fires. While it cures, it gives off smoke and fumes that may bother some people. That's expected and it passes.

  • Keep the room well ventilated. Open all windows and doors during those first fires.
  • Follow the Stove Bright (Forrest Paint) information sheet that came with the stove.
  • Smoke detectors may go off more often while the paint cures, or if the door is left open by accident. Don't disconnect them.

Before the very first fire, remove the retaining clip on the front of the baffle.

The manual strongly recommends smoke and carbon monoxide detectors in the area where the stove is installed.

Learning your stove

Until you're experienced, check the firebox daily for creosote build-up. The right air setting depends on your wood, the outside temperature, your chimney and the weather. With practice, you'll find the settings that suit your home.

ash.title: Removing the ashes
ash.html:
Take ashes out only when the stove is cold, after the fire has burned down and cooled.

  • Empty the firebox whenever the ash gets 3" to 4" deep.
  • Leave about 1" of ash on the firebox bottom. It helps keep a hot charcoal bed.
  • Don't let ash pile up at the front of the firebox. That's where boost combustion air comes in, and heavy ash blocks it.
  • Remove ashes often. Embers can roll out the door and start a fire.

Disposing of ashes

Put ashes in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Set the closed container outside on a non-combustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything that can burn. If you'll bury or spread the ashes, keep them in the closed container until every cinder has cooled completely. Don't put other waste in that container.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
If the glass darkens from slow burning or poor wood, clean it with fireplace glass cleaner once the stove is cold.

  • Never clean the glass while it's hot.
  • Don't use abrasive cleaners, and never scrape it with anything that could scratch.

What the film tells you

A light brown, dusty film that wipes off easily usually means good combustion and dry wood, so your pipes and chimney are fairly clean. A black, greasy film that's hard to remove comes from wet wood and burning too slowly. That deposit is building up at least as fast in your chimney.

Protect the glass

Don't slam the door or knock the glass, and make sure no logs stick out when you close it. Cracked or broken glass must be replaced before you use the stove again. Your dealer supplies the replacement: 9-1/4" x 13-1/4" x 5 mm ceramic glass only.

Hot glass will cause burns. Don't touch it until it has cooled, and never let children touch it.

chimney.title: Creosote and chimney fires
chimney.html:
Slow fires give off tar and vapours that condense in a cool chimney as creosote. If creosote ignites, it burns extremely hot.

  • Have the chimney and connector inspected at least once every two months in the heating season, and cleaned as needed at least twice a year.
  • Remove creosote once it reaches 3 mm or more.
  • To keep it down, burn dry wood and add small loads (two or three logs, or 1/4 to 1/2 of a full load). Leave the air fairly wide open for the first 10 to 30 minutes after loading.

Signs of a chimney fire

Flames and sparks shooting out of the top of the chimney, a roaring sound, or the chimney vibrating.

If it happens

  1. Close down the air inlet on the stove.
  2. Call the fire department.
  3. Get ready to evacuate. Meet at an agreed place outside.
  4. Before the next fire, have the chimney cleaned and checked for stress and cracks.
Keep a fire extinguisher handy and make sure everyone at home knows the plan.

care.title: Maintenance checklist
care.html:
Look for cracks, heavy corrosion, burned-out sections or bad warping.

WeeklyFirebrick (cracks) · door gasket (sagging, placement, damage)
MonthlyBrick rails and tabs · back of the airwash chamber · boost tube cover · top baffle board · baffle tubes
Every 2 monthsChimney inspection
When the chimney is cleanedTop heat shield and mounting bolt · brick rails · manifold
Every six monthsVacuum the optional blower's grill openings (back and bottom of the casing)

Door gasket

The door seals with a 5/8" fiberglass rope gasket that needs only light pressure. Inspect it now and then and replace it if needed, using the gasket kit from your True North dealer.

Baffle

For chimney cleaning, the connector pipe should be taken off the stove. Remove the baffle board only if that isn't possible, and never run the stove with the baffle board or tubes out.

Replace cracked baffle tubes and other damaged parts through your dealer, using only manufacturer-supplied materials. Running the stove with broken parts can damage other parts and will void your warranty.

safety.title: Safety around the stove
safety.html:
• The stove is hot while it's running. Keep children, clothing and furniture away. Touching it can burn skin.
  • Keep the loading door closed while the fire burns. Open it only to add wood. An open door can throw sparks and pull air from your living space.
  • Keep wood, furniture, newspapers and anything else that can burn out of the stove's clearances and the space you need for loading and ash removal.
  • Don't modify the air control. The low burn setting is set at the factory and must not be changed.
  • Teach everyone at home how to run the stove safely and what to do in a chimney fire.

Signs of trouble

Too much draft or over-firing: an uncontrollable burn, or a stove part or the chimney glowing red. Over-firing can permanently damage the stove and chimney and may void the warranty.

Too little draft: smoke puffing back or leaking into the room at the stove or pipe joints.

The manual strongly recommends smoke and carbon monoxide detectors near the stove. Don't disconnect them.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
True North warrants the stove to the original consumer:

Firebox, castings, glass3 years parts (1 year labour)
Electrical components and switches1 year parts and labour
Gaskets, paint (peeling), bricks, baffle tubes, baffle manifold, ceramic fibre board1 year (parts only)

Glass is covered for thermal breakage only, not impact.

Not covered

  • Damage from misuse, abuse, improper installation, lack of maintenance, over-firing, negligence, shipping accidents, power failures, downdrafts or venting problems
  • Scratches, corrosion, warping or discoloration caused by over-firing, abrasives or chemical cleaners
  • Defects or damage from unauthorized parts
  • Service calls related to an improper installation

Making a claim

The warranty isn't transferable, and an authorized qualified technician must install the stove. Give your True North dealer proof of purchase (dated bill of sale), the model name and the serial number. A one-time replacement limit applies to covered parts. You can register the stove at truenorthstoves.com/register.

specOutput.title: Heat output
specOutput.html:
EPA BTU output13,900 to 29,200 btu/hr
Peak BTU/hr output55,000
Maker's website: Heat Output, Cord Wood 60,000 BTU.
FuelSeasoned cord wood

EPA range: CSA B415 efficiency with burn rates from the low and high EPA tests on Douglas Fir dimensional lumber. Peak: maximum one-hour high burn rate from the high-burn EPA test, cord wood at 8600 btu/lb. The introduction (p. 2) states the tested range as 13,931 to 29,208 Btu/hr.

Designed for maximum overall efficiency at a moderate firing rate. Wet wood can cause up to 25% drop in heater output.

specEmissions.title: Emissions & efficiency
specEmissions.html:
EPA certified emissions1.6 grams per hour
HHV tested efficiency72.7%
LHV tested efficiency78%
CO emissions1.56 grams per minute

Efficiencies are weighted averages tested to CSA B415. Meets the EPA 2020 crib wood particulate emission standards (rating label: test Method 28R, 1.6 g/hr). Listed room heater, solid fuel type, to CAN/ULC S627 and UL 1482 (ETL#4001507); also for use in mobile homes.

The manufacturer-set minimum low burn rate must not be altered; doing so is against federal regulations.

specWood.html:
Maximum wood length20 inches

Natural cordwood only, air-dried six months or more. Burn directly on the firebricks; no grates or andirons.

specAir.title: Combustion air
specAir.html:
Direct outside air is necessary for mobile homes and optional for residential installations; consult local code, CAN/CSA-B365 or NFPA 211. The rating label (p. 26) lists the outside air kit as required for mobile home and alcove installations.

Pedestal model

  • Through the floor: leave the rear knockout or cover plate in place; cut a 4"(100mm) or larger hole inside the pedestal perimeter; approved 4"(100mm) inlet vent cap.
  • From behind: hole in the closest exterior wall with an approved 4"(100mm) inlet vent cap; OAIR.1B adapter on the back of the pedestal; 4"(100mm) flexible or rigid metal venting.
  • Room air: remove the knockout or cover plate from the rear of the pedestal.

Leg model

  • Through the floor: 4"(100mm) or larger hole under the stove; OAIR.1B on the underside, connected with 4"(100mm) metal venting; approved inlet vent cap if extended outdoors.
  • From behind: as above, with the adapter on the underside.
  • Room air: remove the knockout or cover plate from the bottom.

Cover floor holes with 20GA wire mesh minimum rodent screen; they must draw from a ventilated crawl space or be ducted outdoors. Outside air requires the stove to be secured to the structure (securing brackets, p. 13).

review.notes: One manual (installation & operation, 28 pages); page numbers are physical PDF pages. Wood stove: no ignition system and no code table (codes empty). Stove dimensions (Figure 1, p. 11) appear only as an unlabeled drawing, so no height/width/depth spec was given. Clearance drawings (Figure 2 p. 12, Figure 8 p. 19) have unlabeled numbers; clearances were taken from the rating label's A-F table (letters defined in text, p. 26). The drawings look like connector-centreline figures (label value + 3 in.), but Figure 8 shows 18 5/8" where Figure 2 shows 18 3/4" (both 475mm) - worth a check. Floor-protector G/H/I values on the label are defined only by its drawing (USA G 16, H 3.5, I 0 in.; Canada G 18, H 8, I 8 in.), so the p. 13 text was used. The 57 3/4" minimum in Figures 6 and 7 (pp. 15-16) has no clear label in the text; not transcribed. Metric equivalents vary slightly between pages (18" = 457 mm p. 13, 455 mm Figure 3, 460 MM label; 12 ft = 3.7 m p. 16, 3.66 m p. 19); inch values agree. p. 2 gives the tested output as 13,931 to 29,208 Btu/hr; p. 3 rounds it to 13,900 to 29,200. The rating label cautions to keep the ash dump closed during firing, but the manual describes no ash dump or ash pan; left out of owner content. p. 9 says to remove the retaining clip on the front of the baffle before the first fire; the clip isn't described further, and the baffle-tube retaining clips on p. 21 are reinstalled, so these may be different parts - confirm. p. 20 calls outside air optional for residential installs, while the label requires the outside air kit for alcove installs; both are shown in specAir. The manual gives no firebox volume, burn time, weight, blower cfm or non-catalytic statement, so catalog firebox_cu_ft, burn_time_hr_max and the blower cfm feature could not be checked. The rating label is bilingual; no French-only safety text needed translating, and no scrambled text was found.
